evidence: I read .github/workflows/release.yml at this PR's merge commit 72eaff8: the step 'Build changelog section and release notes' prepends '## <tag> - <date>' with one bullet per commit, pushes it as 'chore(release): <tag> changelog', and only then tags - so CHANGELOG.md was generated and the hand entry the reviewer asked for would have produced two v0.25.0 headers. The reviewer inferred an authoring convention from entries the workflow itself had written.
guidance_note: A file a workflow writes should say 'generated by <workflow>' in its own header, so neither a reader nor a reviewer can read its history as a hand-authored convention.

evidence: The mutable @master ref is a real supply-chain surface, but the agent's technical counter holds - a reusable workflow runs under the caller's own GITHUB_TOKEN and cannot exceed the contents: write this file already grants - and the mitigation is real: gh api repos/promptctl/.github/branches/master/protection returns required_pull_request_reviews with enforce_admins enabled. The gap the reply does not name is required_approving_review_count: 0, so 'PR-only with admin enforcement' means routed through a PR, not reviewed by a second party.
guidance_note: When declining a hardening finding by pointing at a compensating control, state that control's residual gap in the same reply, so the tradeoff is on the record rather than only the half that favours the decision.

evidence: I fetched promptctl/.github/.github/workflows/release-plugin.yml: it rejects any tag not matching *--v*, then sets name=${tag%%--v*} and version=${tag#*--v}, and matches the changelog with awk -v v="v${version}" against ${dir}/CHANGELOG.md. The prefixed tag never reaches the heading comparison, so the 'no matching section for laws--v0.25.0' failure the reviewer projected cannot occur.
guidance_note: When a call site delegates its implementation to another repo, restate the contract it depends on - here the <name>--v<version> tag shape and the fact that the shared workflow parses it - in a comment at the call site, so the next reader can check it without leaving the repo.

evidence: a9647c1's patch adds 'horizon_need grep' to pin-instrument.sh and verify-instrument.sh while the grep calls live inside lib.sh's horizon_build_memento_snapshot and horizon_lit_next_skill_sha256 - two per-caller declarations of a tool the library reaches for on its callers' behalf, which is the drift HORIZON_BASE_TOOLS' own comment says it exists to prevent.
guidance_note: When a shared library starts invoking a new external tool, add it to the library's own tool list; a need-check written into each caller is a copy that the next caller will forget.

evidence: The reviewer bundled a true claim (the comment asserts the probe is 'the same shape lit will meet at seed time', which the code does not establish - the probe skips populate and commit) with a false one (that this makes the recorded hash disagree with a real run). The agent ran both repo shapes and got the identical sha c1b8329042f6a4a8..., so only the comment half survived; fixing the comment and declining the populate+commit ceremony was the split the thread earned.
guidance_note: When disproving a 'this probe is not representative' premise, enumerate every variable the probe holds fixed against a real run and test each - the agent tested only commit history, and the untested one, the project directory name, came straight back as F4.

evidence: GOAL_PROMPT.md's prose and lib.sh's HORIZON_NEXT_SKILL_REL_PATH both spelled '.claude/skills/next/SKILL.md' and nothing compares them; the manifest and verifier read only the constant, so a future lit writing the procedure elsewhere would leave the prompt pointing at a path that no longer exists while every check stayed green. Deleting the prose copy - the first of the reviewer's two options - leaves one copy and no reconciliation machinery.
guidance_note: Prompt prose should name the artifact the reading agent invokes, never the path a code constant already owns - the harness discovers the skill by name, so the path was only a copy that could rot.

evidence: c9636cd's commit message confirms it rewrote this comment as F2's fix; the rewritten claim still asserted an equivalence tested on only one variable, and the reviewer named the untested one. The agent's own three-name probe shows lit does derive project state from the directory name (issue_prefix=lit / macklebox / some), so the unchecked assumption was real even though the /next bytes happened to match.
guidance_note: A property that holds by luck and is probed under one fixed value at every call site should be re-established by the probe itself - two differently-named probes that must agree, as the agent built - rather than asserted in a comment.

evidence: The race is real: memento_ref and reviewer_sha are resolved once by verify-instrument.sh while goal_ref was resolved from live HEAD inside each pin run. The ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flag is positional, not causal - gh shows the goal_ref line landed in the PR's first commit a9647c1, and c9636cd touched pin-instrument.sh only to delete one 'horizon_need grep' line - so this is a round-0 defect the reviewer reached a round late.
guidance_note: When splitting one pinned identity into two, list the properties the merged form supplied - here resolve-once-by-the-caller, which goal_wording had inherited from memento's sha - and re-establish each of them for both halves.

evidence: The header opened with 'two acceptance criteria' above a three-item list. The flag is a false positive: a9647c1's patch adds criterion 3 and, in the same commit, changes the block's closing line from 'both criteria' to 'every criterion', so the stale count came from the PR's first commit and not from any fix for an earlier finding.
guidance_note: After adding an item to a numbered list, grep the enclosing comment block for its count words ('two', 'both') before leaving the file - the agent updated one of the two and walked past the other three lines above it.

evidence: The README still said verify-instrument.sh 'resolves both moving refs once' after F5's fix made it resolve three and hand all three to both runs; gh shows 9775d5e touched only lib.sh, pin-instrument.sh and verify-instrument.sh, so the doc was left behind by that fix commit.
guidance_note: A fix that adds a control variable is not finished until the same commit updates every place that counts or lists those variables - 9775d5e changed three scripts and no docs, and bought four documentation findings the next round.

evidence: F5's fix added a fourth positional argument defaulting to live HEAD, which made the README's standing promise - pass [reviewer-sha] and 'the manifest is byte-identical across runs on every pinned field' - false, while the top-of-file synopsis still showed only [memento-ref] [reviewer-sha]. gh confirms 9775d5e shipped no README change, so a campaign operator following the doc would have built a racing script.
guidance_note: When a fix changes what a caller must pass to get a documented guarantee, the sentence stating that guarantee is part of the fix, not a follow-up.

evidence: The duplication is real - a branch name owned by promptctl/memento was hardcoded as HORIZON_MEMENTO_DEFAULT_REF and restated in README - but the outage the reviewer feared was not: that repo's default branch is master and the verifier had been fetching it green. Defaulting the ref to the literal HEAD makes the remote answer at fetch time with strictly less machinery than the proposed 'git ls-remote --symref' parse. The commit-flag is positional: the constant landed in a9647c1, not in a fix.
guidance_note: A fact owned by a remote, such as its default branch, should be asked of the remote at use time rather than copied into a constant - HEAD is already the question git accepts, so no name has to be kept in sync.

evidence: Same README line and same undercount as F7 - the reviewer raised it twice in one round - created when F5's fix landed in 9775d5e with no README change. The agent identified the twin thread by id and closed both with one edit, which is the correct handling of a duplicated finding.

F4's fix added the two-probe name-independence check in 9775d5e, a commit gh confirms carried no README change, leaving two README passages describing a single throwaway repo and no documentation for the horizon_die message a maintainer would eventually hit. Sweeping for the class, the agent found a third stale singular in a pin-instrument.sh comment that the reviewer had not reached.
guidance_note: When a fix changes an externally visible behaviour that prose describes - one probe becoming two - grep the tree for every restatement of that behaviour in the same commit, and quote any new error text where a maintainer can grep for it.

evidence: a9647c1 added WORK="$(mktemp -d)" at script scope while horizon_need_base runs inside main(), so a tool ran above the check that establishes it - an original-commit defect, which makes the flag positional. Declining the proposed extra 'horizon_need mktemp' was right (mktemp is already in HORIZON_BASE_TOOLS, so it would be a second checkpoint for one invariant), and moving the need-block above the first tool use in both scripts fixes the class rather than the citation.
guidance_note: Put the tool-availability block at script scope directly after the library is sourced, so 'checked before first use' is enforced by the file's structure instead of by an ordering the author has to remember.

evidence: 7507139 rewrote the README's parallel paragraph to name all three resolved-once refs but changed verify-instrument.sh by a single line (the criteria count), leaving that script's criterion 1 still naming only the reviewer's tag. The same claim lived in two files and the round-2 doc fix swept one of them.
guidance_note: When correcting a claim, grep the tree for the claim's distinctive phrase before committing - 'resolved once' appeared in both the README and the verifier's header, and only the README was fixed.

narrative: One round, one finding, and the agent's no-change pushback was correct: at this PR's merge commit the release workflow generated the CHANGELOG section itself, pushed it as a chore(release) commit and only then tagged, so the hand-written v0.25.0 entry the reviewer asked for would have collided with the generated header. The reviewer's error was reading a generated file's history as evidence of an authoring convention without opening the workflow that wrote it. The reply closed the thread in one pass because it named the exact step and the commit-message shape rather than asserting the conclusion. Fifteen minutes later PR #42 moved the repo to authored changelogs, which does not make this pushback wrong at the time it was made.
guidance_observations: A generated file needs a 'generated by <workflow>' header line; without it the reviewer treats every prior entry as a convention the PR is breaking.
The pushback worked because it cited the mechanism (workflow step name, commit message, ordering) instead of the verdict - that is the shape of a pushback that does not cost a second round.

narrative: Two findings, both pushed back with no change, and both pushbacks hold up: I fetched the shared release-plugin.yml and it parses the tag once into name and version and matches v${version} against the plugin CHANGELOG, so F2's projected breakage cannot occur, and gh confirms promptctl/.github's master carries branch protection with admin enforcement as F1's reply claimed. Both findings have the same root: moving the implementation out of this repo left the reviewer unable to check contracts the change now depends on, so it flagged the unverifiable parts. The agent answered by quoting the external code and running the step verbatim against this tree, which is the right response but leaves the evidence only in a thread.
guidance_observations: When a change delegates its implementation to another repo, restate the depended-on contract at the call site - both findings here were the reviewer asking for exactly that, and a two-line comment would have pre-empted both.
F1's reply named a compensating control (PR-only, admin-enforced) without naming its gap (zero required approvals), which reads more conclusive than the control actually is.

narrative: Thirteen findings across five rounds; every premise was at least partly right and the agent accepted or reshaped all of them except the bug half of F2, which it disproved with a real experiment. Six findings (F4, F7, F8, F10, F11, F13) exist only because an earlier fix landed without its documentation - 9775d5e changed three scripts and no docs, and the following round returned four README findings plus a stale script header. No round is strictly avoidable, though: rounds 1, 2 and 3 each also carried an original-commit defect the reviewer simply reached late (F5's goal_ref race, F6's criteria count and F9's hardcoded branch, F12's mktemp ordering), so the round count is driven by the reviewer's progressive discovery at least as much as by incomplete fixes. Three of the flagged ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT findings (F5, F6, F9, F12) are positional false positives that gh commit diffs settle. The agent's craft was high where it mattered: it verified before accepting (F1), converted an assumption into a per-run check rather than a comment (F4), swept beyond the citation twice (F11, F12), and caught a defect in a comment it had written thirty seconds earlier.
guidance_observations: The dominant self-inflicted cost here is doc-lag inside the review loop: fix commits were code-only, and the docs the agent itself wrote in round 0 became the next round's findings.
F7, F8 and F10 were one change described in three README places and F13 was the same claim in a fourth file - one grep for the phrase being corrected would have closed all four at once.

Comment overclaims were this PR's most reliable finding generator (F2, F4, F6, F7, F8, F10, F11, F13): a comment that asserts an equivalence or a count the code does not establish drew a finding every single round.
The reviewer duplicated a finding across two threads in one round (F7, F10); naming the twin thread id and confirming on both, as the agent did, is the cheapest correct handling.
